subject: Claude CCAF: Tool Design & MCP Integration
description: NEW TOPIC. Choosing local vs project vs user scope, the scope precedence chain, environment variable expansion in .mcp.json, approval and trust behaviour, and verifying tool discovery. Grounded in the official Claude Code MCP documentation.

questions.question: A team wants every developer who clones the repository to get the same Jira MCP server automatically, checked into version control. Which scope and which file?
options: Project scope — the server is written to .mcp.json at the project root, which the team commits.
User scope — the server is written to ~/.claude.json and is available across all projects.
Local scope — the server is written to ~/.claude.json under the project's path.
Managed scope — the server is written to managed-settings.json and pushed by MDM.
questions.answer: Project scope — the server is written to .mcp.json at the project root, which the team commits.
questions.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — MCP: installation scopes
questions.explanation:
The scope table is the fact to memorise. Project scope: loads in the current project only, IS shared with the team via version control, stored in .mcp.json in the project root. The docs add: 'Check .mcp.json into version control so everyone on your team gets the same MCP tools and services.' Add it with claude mcp add --scope project.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** User scope is stored in ~/.claude.json and is explicitly 'private to your user account' — it loads in all YOUR projects, but is shared with nobody.
- **C.** Local scope is the default and is also private to you, loading only in the project where you added it.
- **D.** Managed MCP exists for enterprise deployment, but it is not the mechanism for a team sharing a server through their own repository.
questions.examTrick: Shared with team = project scope = .mcp.json = committed. Everything else in the three-scope table is private to you.

questions.question: You run 'claude mcp add --transport http stripe https://mcp.stripe.com' with no --scope flag. What scope is used and where is the configuration written?
options: Local scope, written to ~/.claude.json under the current project's path.
Project scope, written to .mcp.json at the project root.
User scope, written to ~/.claude.json at the top level.
Local scope, written to .claude/settings.local.json in the project.
questions.answer: Local scope, written to ~/.claude.json under the current project's path.
questions.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — MCP: local scope
questions.explanation:
'Local scope is the default. A local-scoped server loads only in the project where you added it and stays private to you. Claude Code stores it in ~/.claude.json under that project's path, so the same server won't appear in your other projects.' Use it for personal development servers, experimental configurations, or servers with credentials you don't want in version control.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Project scope requires --scope project explicitly; the docs say each add command 'writes to local scope unless you add --scope project or --scope user.'
- **C.** User scope also lives in ~/.claude.json but at the top level, not nested under a project path, and requires --scope user.
- **D.** This is the trap the docs call out by name: 'MCP local-scoped servers are stored in ~/.claude.json (your home directory), while general local settings use .claude/settings.local.json.' Two different files, similar names.
questions.examTrick: Default scope = local = ~/.claude.json keyed by project path. NOT .claude/settings.local.json — different file entirely.

questions.question: A developer has a personal utility MCP server they want available in every project on their machine, but not shared with anyone. Which command?
options: claude mcp add --transport http hubspot --scope user https://mcp.hubspot.com/anthropic
claude mcp add --transport http hubspot --scope project https://mcp.hubspot.com/anthropic
claude mcp add --transport http hubspot --scope local https://mcp.hubspot.com/anthropic
claude mcp add --transport http hubspot --scope global https://mcp.hubspot.com/anthropic
questions.answer: claude mcp add --transport http hubspot --scope user https://mcp.hubspot.com/anthropic
questions.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — MCP: user scope
questions.explanation:
'User-scoped servers are stored in ~/.claude.json and provide cross-project accessibility, making them available across all projects on your machine while remaining private to your user account. This scope works well for personal utility servers, development tools, or services you frequently use across different projects.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Project scope writes .mcp.json into this one repository and is designed to be shared, which is the opposite of both requirements.
- **C.** Local scope loads only in the project where it was added, failing the 'every project' requirement.
- **D.** There is no 'global' scope. The three valid values are local, project, and user.
questions.examTrick: The three scope values are exactly local | project | user. 'global' and 'enterprise' as --scope values are invented distractors.

questions.question: A server named 'analytics' is defined at local scope, in the project's .mcp.json, AND at user scope. Which definition does Claude Code use?
options: The local-scope definition; the entire entry from the highest-precedence source is used and fields are not merged across scopes.
The project-scope definition, since committed team configuration overrides personal configuration.
The user-scope definition, since it is the broadest and loads in all projects.
All three are merged field by field, with local values winning on conflicts.
questions.answer: The local-scope definition; the entire entry from the highest-precedence source is used and fields are not merged across scopes.
questions.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — MCP: scope hierarchy and precedence
questions.explanation:
The documented chain, highest first, is: 1. Local scope, 2. Project scope, 3. User scope, 4. Plugin-provided servers, 5. claude.ai connectors. The docs add: 'When the same server is defined in more than one place, Claude Code connects to it once, using the definition from the highest-precedence source. The entire server entry from that source is used; fields are not merged across scopes.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Note this is the OPPOSITE of settings precedence, where managed/team-level configuration outranks personal. For MCP servers, your local definition wins. Mixing up the two ladders is the classic error.
- **C.** User scope is third of five, below both local and project.
- **D.** Explicitly denied by the docs — no field-level merging. The whole entry comes from one source.
questions.examTrick: MCP precedence: local > project > user > plugin > connector. The three scopes match duplicates by NAME; plugins and connectors match by ENDPOINT.

questions.question: A shared .mcp.json needs to carry an API key without committing the secret. Which syntax does Claude Code support?
options: ${API_KEY} for a plain variable and ${API_BASE_URL:-https://api.example.com} for a variable with a default.
$API_KEY and $(API_BASE_URL||https://api.example.com).
%API_KEY% and %API_BASE_URL:https://api.example.com%.
{{API_KEY}} and {{API_BASE_URL|default:https://api.example.com}}.
questions.answer: ${API_KEY} for a plain variable and ${API_BASE_URL:-https://api.example.com} for a variable with a default.
questions.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — MCP: environment variable expansion in .mcp.json
questions.explanation:
The documented syntax is exactly two forms: '${VAR}: expands to the value of environment variable VAR' and '${VAR:-default}: expands to VAR if set, otherwise uses default'. Expansion is supported in five locations: command, args, env, url, and headers.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, C, D.** These are shell, Windows cmd, and templating-language syntaxes respectively. None is what .mcp.json parses. The exam supplies plausible-looking alternatives from adjacent ecosystems.

One more documented behaviour worth knowing: if a referenced variable is not set and has no default, the config still loads — Claude Code reports a missing-variable warning for that server in 'claude mcp list' and uses the unexpanded ${VAR} text as-is. It does not fail the whole file.
questions.examTrick: Only ${VAR} and ${VAR:-default}. Expandable in command, args, env, url, headers. Missing var = warning + literal text, not a hard failure.

questions.question: In which fields of a .mcp.json server entry does Claude Code perform environment variable expansion?
options: command, args, env, url, and headers.
env only, since that is the environment block.
command and args only, since those are executed.
Every string value anywhere in the file, including the server name.
questions.answer: command, args, env, url, and headers.
questions.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — MCP: expansion locations
questions.explanation:
The docs list the expansion locations exactly: command (the server executable path), args (command-line arguments), env (environment variables passed to the server), url (for HTTP server types), and headers (for HTTP server authentication).

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Too narrow — this misses the two that matter most for remote servers, url and headers, which is where a Bearer token typically goes.
- **C.** Too narrow in the other direction; it covers only stdio servers.
- **D.** Expansion is scoped to those five fields, not applied blanket-wise across the document.
questions.examTrick: Five fields: command, args, env, url, headers. Remember url + headers — that is how remote servers get their auth without committing it.

questions.question: After adding an MCP server, what is the correct way to verify Claude Code actually connected and discovered its tools?
options: Run /mcp in a session, or 'claude mcp list' / 'claude mcp get <name>', and check the connection status.
Check that 'claude mcp add' printed its 'Added ...' line, which confirms the connection succeeded.
Grep ~/.claude.json for the server name to confirm the entry exists.
Restart Claude Code; a server that fails to connect prevents startup, so a successful launch is the confirmation.
questions.answer: Run /mcp in a session, or 'claude mcp list' / 'claude mcp get <name>', and check the connection status.
questions.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — MCP: server status
questions.explanation:
The docs draw this distinction sharply: 'claude mcp add confirms a successful add by printing an Added ... line, which means the configuration was WRITTEN. claude mcp list then shows a health status next to each server it lists, such as ✔ Connected, ! Needs authentication, or ✘ Failed to connect.' They also note 'The claude mcp add command saves the configuration without validating credentials, so a placeholder value is accepted here but the server fails to connect later.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** This is the exact misconception the docs correct: 'Added' means written, not connected.
- **C.** Presence of the entry says nothing about whether the server starts, authenticates, or exposes tools.
- **D.** A failed server does not block startup; it simply shows a failure status.
questions.examTrick: 'Added' = config written. /mcp or 'claude mcp list' = actually connected. The exam tests that gap.

questions.question: A project-scoped server from .mcp.json shows as '⏸ Pending approval' in claude mcp list. Why, and what resolves it?
options: Claude Code prompts for approval before using project-scoped servers from .mcp.json for security reasons; run claude interactively to review and approve.
The server's OAuth token expired; run /mcp and re-authenticate.
The server was added at the wrong scope; re-add it with --scope local.
The .mcp.json file has a syntax error; fix the JSON and restart.
questions.answer: Claude Code prompts for approval before using project-scoped servers from .mcp.json for security reasons; run claude interactively to review and approve.
questions.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — MCP: project scope approvals
questions.explanation:
'For security reasons, Claude Code prompts for approval in interactive sessions before using project-scoped servers from .mcp.json files. To reset those approval choices, run claude mcp reset-project-choices.' The rationale is that .mcp.json arrives from a repository other people can write to.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Authentication problems show as '! Needs authentication', a different status.
- **C.** Re-adding at local scope would sidestep the prompt but is not the intended fix, and it would break the team-sharing goal.
- **D.** A malformed file would not produce a per-server pending-approval status.

Important related fact: 'claude -p runs, Agent SDK sessions, and cloud sessions can't show that prompt: Claude Code loads project-scoped servers there without asking.' To keep a server out anyway, add it to disabledMcpjsonServers, which blocks it in every mode.
questions.examTrick: Only PROJECT-scoped (.mcp.json) servers need approval, because they come from the repo. Headless/-p sessions load them without asking.

questions.question: Engineers keep copy-pasting Jira ticket descriptions and comments into conversations during code review. The team wants Claude to access this standard Jira data directly. What is the most effective approach?
options: Integrate an existing Jira MCP server that exposes tickets and comments as discoverable tools.
Use the Bash tool with curl to call Jira's REST API, including auth headers and parsing JSON inline.
Export Jira tickets to markdown files in the repository that Claude reads with the Read tool.
Build a custom MCP server tailored precisely to this team's Jira workflow.
questions.answer: Integrate an existing Jira MCP server that exposes tickets and comments as discoverable tools.
questions.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — MCP: what you can do; build-vs-use guidance
questions.explanation:
The docs give the trigger verbatim: 'Connect a server when you find yourself copying data into chat from another tool, like an issue tracker or a monitoring dashboard.' For a standard integration with well-maintained community servers, use the existing server rather than building. An MCP server exposes tickets and comments as discoverable tools with structured descriptions, handled auth, and standardised error reporting.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Bash plus curl bypasses the tool interface entirely: hand-rolled auth headers, inline JSON parsing every time, no tool description and no standardised error handling.
- **C.** An export goes stale the moment a ticket is updated, and the team wants live data rather than a snapshot.
- **D.** Building custom is the right call only for a workflow with no community equivalent. Ordinary ticket data does not justify the maintenance burden.
questions.examTrick: 'Copying data from another tool into chat' is the canonical MCP trigger. Community server first; custom build only where no equivalent exists.

questions.question: When adding a stdio MCP server, what is the purpose of the -- (double dash) in 'claude mcp add [options] <name> -- <command> [args...]'?
options: It separates Claude's own options (--transport, --env, --scope) from the command and arguments that run the server; everything after it is passed to the server untouched.
It marks the end of the server name and the start of the transport URL.
It escapes the command so the shell does not expand environment variables in it.
It is optional syntactic sugar retained for compatibility with older CLI versions.
questions.answer: It separates Claude's own options (--transport, --env, --scope) from the command and arguments that run the server; everything after it is passed to the server untouched.
questions.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — MCP: installing servers
questions.explanation:
The docs flag this as 'Important: Separate server arguments with --'. For stdio servers, the double dash separates Claude's own options from the command and arguments that run the server. Everything after -- is passed to the server untouched. Example: claude mcp add --transport stdio myserver -- npx server runs 'npx server'.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** stdio servers have no URL; the transport is chosen with --transport.
- **C.** It is an argument-boundary marker, not a shell-escaping device.
- **D.** Without it, flags meant for the server would be consumed by Claude's own argument parser — it is functionally required, not decorative.
questions.examTrick: -- is the boundary between Claude's flags and the server's own command line. Required for stdio adds with server-side flags.

questions.question: Which transport flag do you use for a remote MCP server at an https:// endpoint that the instructions say uses SSE?
options: --transport sse
--transport http
--transport ws
--transport stdio
questions.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — MCP: from a URL
questions.explanation:
'For an https:// endpoint, add it with --transport http, or with --transport sse when the instructions say the endpoint uses SSE.' Both are https URLs; the distinction is what the server speaks.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Correct for a plain HTTP MCP endpoint, but the question specifies SSE.
- **C.** The docs state --transport doesn't accept 'ws'; a wss:// endpoint uses the separate 'add a remote WebSocket server' option.
- **D.** stdio is for locally-executed server processes, not remote URLs.
questions.examTrick: https + plain = http; https + SSE = sse; wss = the separate WebSocket option, NOT --transport ws; local process = stdio.

questions.question: How should a permission rule, skill allowed-tools list, or hook matcher reference a tool from an MCP server named 'database-tools'?
options: By its full namespaced name, mcp__database-tools__<tool>, and for a plugin-bundled server the matcher must account for the plugin's namespacing.
By the bare tool name as the server exposes it, since Claude Code resolves the server automatically.
By the server name alone, database-tools, which covers all of its tools.
By the transport-qualified name, http__database-tools__<tool>.
questions.answer: By its full namespaced name, mcp__database-tools__<tool>, and for a plugin-bundled server the matcher must account for the plugin's namespacing.
questions.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — MCP: tool naming; plugin-bundled servers
questions.explanation:
MCP tools use the mcp__<server>__<tool> form, and the docs say to 'Use this full name when referencing the tool in permission rules, a skill's allowed-tools list, a subagent's tools field, or a hook matcher.' They add a specific gotcha: 'A hook matcher written against the bare server key, such as mcp__database-tools__.*, never fires for a plugin-bundled server' — a plugin's server registers under plugin:<plugin-name>:<server-name>.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Bare names are ambiguous across servers and are not what the permission and hook matchers see.
- **C.** The server name alone is not a tool reference; you would need a glob such as mcp__database-tools__* (valid for allow, since the server segment is literal).
- **D.** Transport is not part of any tool name.
questions.examTrick: mcp__<server>__<tool> everywhere. Plugin-bundled servers register as plugin:<plugin>:<server>, so bare-server matchers silently never fire.

questions.question: A .mcp.json server references ${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR} in its args. Why does the documentation recommend writing ${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR:-.} instead?
options: The variable is set in the server's environment, not Claude Code's own, so a project- or local-scoped entry needs a default to expand correctly.
The variable was renamed and the default provides backwards compatibility.
Defaults are mandatory for every expansion in .mcp.json; a bare ${VAR} is a syntax error.
The default prevents the path from being redacted when it contains a credential.
questions.answer: The variable is set in the server's environment, not Claude Code's own, so a project- or local-scoped entry needs a default to expand correctly.
questions.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — MCP: CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR
questions.explanation:
The docs state: 'This variable is set in the server's environment, not in Claude Code's own environment, so referencing it via ${VAR} expansion in the command or args of a project-scoped .mcp.json entry or a local- or user-scoped server entry in ~/.claude.json requires a default such as ${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR:-.}. Plugin-provided MCP configurations substitute ${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR} directly and don't need the default.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** No rename is involved.
- **C.** A bare ${VAR} is perfectly valid syntax; without a default and without the variable set, you get a warning and the literal text.
- **D.** Redaction applies to credential-named variables passed to a headersHelper, an unrelated mechanism.
questions.examTrick: ${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR} needs :-. in .mcp.json and ~/.claude.json entries. Plugin-provided configs substitute it directly.

questions.question: Which statement about MCP servers and the context window is correct?
options: Tool names and server instructions load at session start; full JSON schemas stay deferred until Claude needs a specific tool.
All connected servers' full tool schemas load into context at session start.
Nothing loads until Claude calls a tool, so idle servers have exactly zero context cost.
MCP tool schemas load only inside subagents, keeping the main conversation free of them.
questions.answer: Tool names and server instructions load at session start; full JSON schemas stay deferred until Claude needs a specific tool.
questions.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Extend Claude Code: context cost by feature
questions.explanation:
The context-cost table lists MCP servers as loading at session start with 'Tool names; full schemas on demand', giving a cost of 'Low until a tool is used'. Tool search is on by default, so idle MCP tools consume minimal context. Run /context all to see how many tokens each loaded MCP tool uses.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** This was the concern that tool search and deferred schemas were built to solve; it is not current behaviour.
- **C.** 'Minimal' is not 'zero' — names and server instructions do load. Hooks are the feature with genuinely zero context cost unless they return output.
- **D.** Subagents get their own context, but that has nothing to do with where MCP schemas load.
questions.examTrick: MCP at startup = names only, schemas deferred. Zero-context feature = hooks. Full content at startup = CLAUDE.md.

questions.question: An MCP server in a project's .mcp.json uses headersHelper to generate auth headers. When does Claude Code run that helper?
options: Only after you accept the trust dialog for the folder you started the session in; until then it connects with static headers alone.
Immediately at session start, since the helper is needed to establish the connection.
Only in interactive sessions; headless -p runs skip it entirely.
Once per machine at install time, with the result cached in ~/.claude.json.
questions.answer: Only after you accept the trust dialog for the folder you started the session in; until then it connects with static headers alone.
questions.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — MCP: trust a folder before its headersHelper runs
questions.explanation:
'Claude Code executes a headersHelper as an arbitrary shell command. For a server in a project .mcp.json or at local scope, it runs the helper only after you accept the trust dialog for the folder you started the session in.' Until you trust the folder, Claude Code connects the server with its static headers alone. Notably, a parent folder's trust does not count.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** That would execute repository-supplied shell code before you had approved the repository — precisely the risk the trust gate exists to prevent.
- **C.** Headless runs are not exempt from the trust rule; they print a 'headersHelper not run' line per server to stderr telling you how to grant the trust.
- **D.** 'Claude Code runs the helper fresh on each connection, at session start and on reconnect... It doesn't cache the result.'
questions.examTrick: headersHelper = arbitrary shell code from the repo, so it is trust-gated and re-run on every connection, never cached.

questions.question: Your organization's security team approved a narrow subset of an MCP server's OAuth scopes. What is the supported way to pin them?
options: Set oauth.scopes to a single space-separated string in the server's configuration; it takes precedence over discovered metadata.
Set oauth.scopes to an array of scope strings in managed-settings.json.
Add a deny rule for each tool that requires an unapproved scope.
Set authServerMetadataUrl, which is the only supported way to constrain scopes.
questions.answer: Set oauth.scopes to a single space-separated string in the server's configuration; it takes precedence over discovered metadata.
questions.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — MCP: restrict OAuth scopes
questions.explanation:
'Set oauth.scopes to pin the scopes Claude Code requests during the authorization flow. This is the supported way to restrict an MCP server to a security-team-approved subset... The value is a single space-separated string, matching the scope parameter format in RFC 6749 §3.3.' It takes precedence over both authServerMetadataUrl and the scopes discovered at /.well-known.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** The value is a space-separated string, not an array — a format detail the exam likes.
- **C.** Deny rules control which tools Claude may call, not which OAuth scopes are requested at authorization time. The token would still be over-privileged.
- **D.** Backwards: oauth.scopes takes precedence over authServerMetadataUrl, and metadata discovery is a fallback, not the control.

Also worth knowing: if the authorization server advertises offline_access, Claude Code appends it to the pinned scopes so the token can refresh. And a 403 insufficient_scope triggers re-authentication with the same pinned scopes.
questions.examTrick: oauth.scopes = ONE space-separated string, wins over metadata discovery. Not an array, not a deny rule.

questions.question: You want to add an MCP server from a JSON block written for another client's settings file, storing it in your user configuration. Which approach is documented?
options: Use claude mcp add-json with --scope user, ensuring the JSON is properly escaped for your shell and conforms to the MCP server configuration schema.
Paste the mcpServers block directly into ~/.claude/settings.json under a mcpServers key.
Convert it to a .mcp.json at the project root; that is the only file that accepts raw JSON blocks.
Use claude mcp import, which reads any client's configuration format automatically.
questions.answer: Use claude mcp add-json with --scope user, ensuring the JSON is properly escaped for your shell and conforms to the MCP server configuration schema.
questions.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — MCP: add servers from JSON configuration
questions.explanation:
The docs cover add-json for exactly this input shape, with three tips: make sure the JSON is properly escaped in your shell, the JSON must conform to the MCP server configuration schema, and 'You can use --scope user to add the server to your user configuration instead of the project-specific one.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** MCP servers are not configured in settings.json; user- and local-scope servers live in ~/.claude.json, and project servers in .mcp.json.
- **C.** .mcp.json is the project-scope store, not a universal paste target, and using it would share the server with the team.
- **D.** 'claude mcp import' in the docs refers specifically to importing from Claude Desktop on macOS and WSL, not to arbitrary client formats.
questions.examTrick: A pasted mcpServers JSON block = claude mcp add-json, and it defaults to local scope unless you pass --scope.

questions.question: An organization needs a server available to everyone with a configuration that user and project settings cannot override. Which mechanism, and how does it relate to the three installation scopes?
options: Managed MCP configuration, deployed at the enterprise level, which sits outside and above the local/project/user scope chain.
Project scope committed to .mcp.json, since a committed file is authoritative for the repository.
User scope pushed to every machine by MDM, since user scope loads in all projects.
Local scope written by a provisioning script, since local scope has the highest precedence.
questions.answer: Managed MCP configuration, deployed at the enterprise level, which sits outside and above the local/project/user scope chain.
questions.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — MCP: installation scopes; managed MCP configuration
questions.explanation:
The scopes section states: 'MCP servers can be configured at three scopes... Administrators can also deploy servers at the enterprise level via managed configuration.' Managed MCP is the enterprise tier and is what you use when the configuration must not be overridable.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** A committed .mcp.json is overridden by any developer's local-scope server of the same name, since local sits above project in the precedence chain.
- **C.** User scope is third of five in the chain, below both local and project, so it is the easiest to override.
- **D.** Local scope does have the highest precedence of the three, but it is per-developer and per-project, which makes it the wrong tool for an organization-wide guarantee — and it is the developer's own file to edit.
questions.examTrick: The three named scopes are all user-editable. 'Cannot be overridden / organization-wide' = managed MCP, the enterprise tier.
